title: Threads and the thread pool
summary: What a thread costs, how the pool hands threads out and grows, and why a pool thread must never sit and wait.

steps.title: A thread is expensive; the pool shares them
body: A **thread** is the operating system's unit of execution: its own stack (1 MB reserved by default on Windows), its own registers,
and a slot in the OS scheduler. Creating one costs tens of microseconds; switching between threads costs a few microseconds each time.
A web service cannot afford a new thread per request.
So .NET keeps a **thread pool**: a small set of worker threads that take **work items** off a queue and run them. `Task.Run`, the
continuation after an `await`, ASP.NET Core request handling and timer callbacks are all work items on that pool.
Console.WriteLine(Thread.CurrentThread.IsThreadPoolThread);   // False: Main runs on its own thread
How many workers? The pool starts with **one per CPU core** (`ThreadPool.GetMinThreads`). Up to that minimum it creates a thread
immediately when work is waiting. Above it, a *hill-climbing* algorithm adds threads slowly, about **one or two per second**, and only
when the queue is not draining. That slowness is deliberate: more threads than cores usually means more switching, not more work done.

steps.prompt: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: a piece of code queued for a pool thread to run
the number the pool creates at once, without waiting (one per core by default)
the pool adding threads slowly while the queue is not draining
the OS saving one thread's registers and loading another's

steps.title: Waiting is not working
body: A request handler spends most of its time **waiting**: for the database, an HTTP call, a file. What matters is what the thread does
- **Blocking** (`Thread.Sleep`, `.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, a synchronous database call): the thread sits
there, doing nothing, and no other work item can use it.
- **Awaiting** (`await db.QueryAsync()`): the method returns its thread to the pool. When the result arrives, a pool thread (any one)
picks the method up again where it left off.
With awaiting, eight threads can serve thousands of requests that are mostly waiting. With blocking, each waiting request holds a
thread, and the 9th request waits for the pool to grow, one thread per second or so. That is **thread-pool starvation**.

steps.prompt: A pool thread runs `var customer = repo.GetCustomerAsync(id).Result;` and the database takes 400 ms. What is that thread doing for those 400 ms?
options: Nothing useful: it is blocked, and no other work item can run on it
It runs other requests until the result arrives, then comes back
It returns to the pool, like `await` does
It spins at 100% CPU checking the task
explain: `.Result` blocks the calling thread until the task completes (after a brief spin, it sleeps on an event). The thread is held for the
whole 400 ms. `await` is what gives the thread back.

steps.explain: The program's main thread is not a pool thread. `Task.Run` queues the lambda as a work item, so it runs on a pool worker.

steps.prompt: Inside an ASP.NET Core request handler: does this hold the thread while it waits?
steps.explain: Anything that waits synchronously (`.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, `Thread.Sleep`, `SemaphoreSlim.Wait`) keeps the thread. The `...Async` version awaited gives it back.

steps.title: Give the thread back while the database works
prompt: This handler looks up a customer's name and blocks on `.Result` while it waits. Under load it is the reason the service stalls.
Rewrite `HandleAsync(Db db, int id)` so that it **awaits** `db.LoadNameAsync(id)` instead of blocking, and returns
The tests call `HandleAsync` while the fake database has not answered yet. A version that blocks cannot return until the database
answers (the tests give up after two seconds); a version that awaits returns an unfinished task straight away.
starter: static Task<string> HandleAsync(Db db, int id)
solution: static async Task<string> HandleAsync(Db db, int id)
template: Dojo.Check("HandleAsync returns while the database is still working", !dojoTask.IsCompleted,
"It only returned after the database answered: something blocks the thread (.Result, .Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()).");
Dojo.Eq("HandleAsync(db, 7) gives the customer line", "customer 7: Dana", await dojoTask);
public Db() => _ = Task.Delay(2000).ContinueWith(_ => Answer());   // a blocked caller is released after 2 s

forbid.message: Does not block on the task

hints: Mark the method `async` and use `await` where it now uses `.Result`.
`static async Task<string> HandleAsync(Db db, int id) { var name = await db.LoadNameAsync(id); return $"customer {id}: {name}"; }`
explain: Notice how the test is built: the fake database does not answer until the test says so. That makes "does it block?" a deterministic
question instead of a timing guess. You will use the same trick (a `TaskCompletionSource` as a gate) to test concurrent code all through
